newsitem.title: UK: No broad commodity trend seen in 1997 - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: No broad commodity trend seen in 1997 - Merrill.

text.p: The first half of 1997 is likely to be similar to 1996 in commodity markets with areas of sector strength and weakness based on the fundamentals of individual commodities, Merrill Lynch said.

But in its 1997 Year Ahead outlook for world commodity marklets the brokerage house said that non-financial commodity prices are in a long-term "demand-driven" uptrend, moving towards the turn of the century.
The performance of the inflation-sensitive gold market presents a bearish picture, with a mixed to lower outlook.

"In fact, we see the potential for as much as a $20 decline in gold prices in coming months, which reinforces our confidence that commodities are unlikely to upset the current benign inflation atmosphere," the broker said.
Oil, meanwhile, will see robust global demand growth which will allow for the return of Iraqi crude and increases in non-OPEC output.
In the metal markets, Merrill said that copper is entering a decade of high average prices and hign price volatility, driven by very rapid consumption growth.
"China in general, and the Chinese State Reserve Bureau in particular will continue to be the copper market's wild cards," it said.
Aluminium prices should improve in 1997 on re-stocking demand, and the downside looks fairly limited.
Zinc's outlook for 1997 and 1998 is bullish, as already positive fundamentals improve, but the lead market is being swamped by Chinese exports.
Average prices this year will be much lower than would otherwise be the case, although the market will be steady.
Nickel's outlook is not expected to pick up until the second half of the year when stainless-steel scrap dries up and mills have to buy more primary nickel, it said.
Tin is unlikely to excite in 1997, as production is expected to rise by 10,000 to 20,000 tonnes while many producers do not like to see high prices as these kill off long-term consumption prospects.
In agricultural commodities, Merrill expects heavy selling by coffee producers in the first quarter of 1997, but for supplies to tighten after that.
Meanwhile, uncertainty over crop sizes will keep the cocoa market in quiet ranges during the first part of next year, but mounting stocks will bear down on sugar, Merrill added.
